Read a rate feed

A core node tells anyone who asks what it converts at, in a small signed UDP datagram. This page shows how to subscribe to one, check every datagram before you believe it, and read the rates.

Early days. Dassie takes test money only: a node refuses the live realm. How far along it is

What a feed says

A feed lists the settlement methods the node's peers pay it on, each by its scheme's ID, such as hub-xrpl-testnet-xrp, with the largest packet the node takes on it. For each pair of methods it converts between, it gives a rate, and it gives the fee it takes on everything it passes on. The node signs the feed with its node key and sends it to every subscriber: at most once a second while its rates move, and every thirty seconds otherwise, so you know it is still there. Each feed says until when it counts.

Market makers read feeds to find nodes whose rates make a trade worth it, which nudges those nodes' holdings back toward balance. dassie market-maker is one such reader; see Run a market maker. How a node sets its rates is on Exchange rates, and every byte of the format is on Rate feed wire format.

Only a core node, one with a domain name, publishes a feed. A node without one has nowhere to be found at, so it publishes nothing.

Why a signed UDP feed: cheap for the node, and checkable by anyone.

Subscribing and the cookie

UDP lets anyone write any sender address, so a node sends its feed only to an address that has shown it receives there. That proof is a cookie: a short value the node hands you, made from your address, that you send back.

  1. Find the node. Fetch its discovery document, https://<host>/.well-known/dassie/node. It names the node's id, its two public keys, publicKey and slhDsaPublicKey in base64url, and the feed's UDP port as feedPort. 

    $curl https://node.example/.well-known/dassie/node
{"id":"…","publicKey":"…","slhDsaPublicKey":"…","feedPort":7768}

    Check that the ID is the hash of the two keys before you trust either (the reader below shows how). No feedPort means the node publishes no feed. Programs that read the network's link states find the port there too, in the node's own entry.

  2. Ask for the feed. Send a Subscribe without a cookie to that port on the node's host, from the socket you will read on. It is 64 bytes: version 02, tag 80, 80 for "no cookie", then zeros.

  3. Take the cookie. The node answers with a Challenge, 18 bytes: 02 81 and a 16-byte cookie. Send a Subscribe at once with that cookie in it: 02 80 81, the cookie, then zeros to 64 bytes.

  4. Read feeds. The node sends you its latest feed right away, then every new one. Take datagrams only from the node's address and port.

  5. Renew every minute. Send the Subscribe with your latest cookie once a minute. Whenever a Challenge comes, take its cookie and send a Subscribe at once. A subscription you stop renewing lapses after a few minutes, and a node that restarts forgets every cookie, so it challenges you again.

A node never answers an address it has not proven with more bytes than it got, which is why a Subscribe is padded. It keeps a bounded list of subscribers, and only a few per IPv4 address or IPv6 /56. When the list is full, a newcomer gets nothing and tries again at its next renewal.

Checking each datagram

A Feed datagram is 02 82, the length of the feed, the feed's bytes, and a 64-byte Ed25519 signature over exactly those bytes. Take a feed only if all of these hold:

  • It decodes. The version byte is 02, and nothing follows the signature. The feed is canonical OER, every value with one encoding; refuse anything else.
  • It is a feed. Its bytes start with the feed's object identifier, 0d 2b 06 01 04 01 83 a8 78 05 8a 77 03 02, so a feed's signature never passes for anything else the node signs.
  • It is this node's. The 32-byte key that follows is the publicKey of the node you subscribed to.
  • The signature verifies under that key, over the feed's bytes as received. Dassie verifies by the ZIP-215 rules and refuses small-order keys; a key a node derives from its phrase is never one.
  • It is newer. Its sequence, in milliseconds, is larger than the last feed you took, so a replayed or late datagram never sets the rates back.
  • It still counts. Now is before its validUntil. With no feed that counts, assume nothing about the node's rates.

A feed is signed, not encrypted: it says nothing a node's packets would not.

Reading the rates

Methods come in ascending order of their IDs, and each rate names two of them by their place in that list: the method a packet comes in on, and the one it leaves on. A rate is what one unit in gets out, in the units of each method's ledger, times 1015, the node's spread included. A packet that comes in with amount goes out with at most: 

fee = floor(amount × feePpm / 1,000,000)
out = floor((amount − fee) × rate / 10^15)

"At most", because the rate is what a vanishingly small packet gets. A real packet also pays for its own effect on the node's holdings, so the larger it is against the node's value, the less it gets. A pair the node does not convert right now is left out, and a rate is never zero.

So a feed is a reason to ask, not a price to count on. Before you trade, quote the payment through the node, and pay only if the quote still works for you.

A small reader

This Node.js script fetches a node's discovery document, checks its ID, subscribes, and prints every feed that passes the checks above. It uses only Node's own modules. Run it with node feed.mjs https://node.example.

Node's Ed25519 follows RFC 8032 rather than ZIP-215. The two agree on every signature a node makes; they differ only on odd signatures no node writes. In Rust, the dassie-feed crate has a subscriber's side, FeedReceiver, that does every check. It lives in the repository and is not on crates.io.

Test vectors

testdata/feed/vectors.json pins the format. All its datagrams are signed with one fixed key, whose publicKey, slhDsaPublicKey and nodeId it gives, so you can check your ID code too. It holds:

  • two Subscribes, with and without a cookie, and a Challenge;
  • three feeds your reader must take, with their decoded fields: a heartbeat with no methods, one with two methods, and the largest the format allows, eight methods and a rate for every pair;
  • four it must refuse, each with the reason: a tampered signature, a feed signed by another key, a small-order key, and a datagram of version 1.

The heartbeat and two-method feeds have expired, and the largest is valid until the largest u64, so test your decoding and signature check with the vectors, and your clock check apart. Dassie's own code makes the vectors, since no other implementation exists yet; running its generator again gives the same file. A changed vector would mean a new feed version.

When nothing arrives

  • No feedPort in the discovery document: the node has no domain name, or no UDP socket for its feed.
  • No Challenge comes back: a firewall drops UDP to the port, on the node's side or yours. The default port is 7768.
  • Challenges, but no feed: check that your Subscribe carries the cookie and comes from the same address and port the Challenge went to. If it does, the node's list may be full, or your address may hold its share already; renew and wait.
  • Feeds with no methods: the node is alive, but has no fresh exchange rates right now, or offers its peers no settlement method yet.

If you run the node, sudo dassie status has a line for its feed: where it serves, to how many subscribers, and what it sent and took. Under systemd the feed's socket is dassie-feed.socket, on UDP port 7768; open it in your firewall. See Check on your node and Files, ports and sockets.
